scope: Verified bibliography and own critical reading notes; no reproduction of copyrighted full texts

papers.title: Technology advancement is driving electric vehicle adoption
papers.sample: Weighted new-vehicle-buyer discrete-choice surveys2012–2013 and2020–2021; second survey734 car and862 SUV responses
papers.method: Repeated stated-choice experiments and heterogeneous choice modeling; attribute/technology versus preference comparison
papers.finding: Technology improvements, including range and reduced BEV price premium, stronger driver than preference changes; no statistically significant preference shift over the decade in main analysis
papers.limitation: Stated rather than completed purchases; US not Germany; non-significance is not proof of identical preferences; no Tesla causal elasticity; projections depend on availability/technology scenarios
papers.implication: Control observable product improvement before interpreting coefficient drift as changing tastes; retain constant-coefficient comparison

papers.title: An in-depth examination of electric vehicle incentives: Consumer heterogeneity and changing response over time
papers.sample: Survey of more than14000 electric-vehicle purchasers2010–2017
papers.method: Buyer surveys on purchase intentions, demographics and incentives over time
papers.finding: Incentives become more important as adoption moves beyond early adopters; incentive importance varies between buyers
papers.limitation: Only abstract read; self-reported hypothetical absence-of-incentive responses; selected EV purchasers, not population panel or German price experiment
papers.implication: Buyer composition and incentive regime can change aggregate response; test heterogeneity without imposing phase boundaries

papers.title: Who will buy electric vehicles after early adopters? Using machine learning to identify the electric vehicle mainstream market
papers.method: Cross-sectional consumer survey; k-means six clusters
papers.finding: Price central to potential mainstream adoption, alongside technology/status and other attributes;85percent of Blue-collar Moderates consider cars below30000EUR in that historical survey
papers.limitation: Potential adoption and clustering, not causal price elasticity; no Germany; historical nominal thresholds not current German cutoffs; not an observed temporal transition
papers.implication: Use price, range and segments separately; do not assume brand/status disappears as market grows

papers.title: Willingness-to-pay for alternative fuel vehicle characteristics: A stated choice study for Germany
papers.method: Germany-wide discrete choice experiment; latent-class model with six consumer segments
papers.finding: Willingness to pay differs across groups and attributes must meet minimum requirements to enter consideration
papers.limitation: Abstract read, not final full text; stated choices; historical market; alternative-fuel vehicles broader than BEVs; unrelated RWTH search PDF not treated as this paper
papers.implication: Price per100km range alone loses attribute thresholds and consumer heterogeneity

papers.title: Charged up? Preferences for Electric Vehicle Charging and Implications for Charging Infrastructure Planning
papers.method: Conditional logit with respondent fixed effects; hypothetical charging bundles
papers.finding: Charging location, duration and waiting matter jointly with cost; home charging valued over alternatives
papers.limitation: FCN Working Paper3/2019; hypothetical choices not purchases; not the Hackbarth2016 title suggested by initial search; no direct new-car sales elasticity
papers.implication: Include charging access as a constraint or interaction, not only fuel-price savings

papers.title: Early adopters of electric vehicles in Germany unveiled
papers.sample: 3111 owner responses; contacted more than9200 owners; surveyDecember2013–February2014; includesBEV/PHEV/lightEV
papers.method: Survey of actual EV holders, with adopter subgroup comparisons
papers.finding: EV users heterogeneous in socioeconomic characteristics, motivation and charging/driving behavior
papers.limitation: Actual ownership but motivations self-reported; response/selection effects; early historical cohort and mixed vehicle types; not a longitudinal shift to2026
papers.implication: Separate vehicle/owner types; do not extrapolate one early-adopter profile to all current buyers

papers.title: How to trigger mass market adoption of electric vehicles? Factors predicting interest in electric vehicles in Germany
papers.sample: 1017 adult respondentsApril2013;14 innovators/early adopters,468 majority,535 laggards
papers.method: Logistic interest model with manual stepwise variable elimination and k-means clusters
papers.finding: Technology affinity and perceived fit to driving needs associated with interest; independence associated with conventional cars negatively related
papers.limitation: Interest not purchase; only14 early adopters; post-selection uncertainty and exploratory clustering; cannot identify evolving German price sensitivity
papers.implication: Use qualitative hypotheses; do not import post-selected coefficients or phase proportions as priors

papers.title: Network Externality and Subsidy Structure in Two-Sided Markets: Evidence from Electric Vehicle Incentives
papers.sample: Vehicle registry and charging market2010–2015 as described by publisher
papers.method: Two-sided market framework with indirect network effects and counterfactual policy analysis
papers.finding: Positive link between purchases and both price and charging subsidies; relative policy efficiency changes with scale
papers.limitation: Full article not accessed; linked PDF endpoint returned HTML; structural assumptions and Norwegian setting not independently replicated; no German elasticity imported
papers.implication: Price and charging deployment jointly determined; infrastructure is not merely a nuisance control

access_note: Full text denotes accessed and consulted text, not exhaustive replication or a guarantee of methodological validity; abstract-only sources remain explicit.
